prime.problem: A paper's disaggregated fleet is sized once for one workload. A real cluster has to pick hardware per phase, decide per request where the KV and the work go, resize the pools as traffic moves, and admit when splitting isn't worth it at all.
prime.fits: Third card of the disaggregation block, after DistServe I and II. It skims Splitwise (hardware per phase, layer-wise transfer), recaps Mooncake from course 4 (a pooled KV store), and walks Dynamo (router, planner, NIXL), then applies Kiely's thresholds.
expect: Splitwise's phase characterization and heterogeneous pools
Dynamo's KV-aware router cost and planner
prime.goal: Decide whether a given workload should be disaggregated, and if so explain which hardware, routing and transfer choices a production system makes and why.

attend: Why can the token phase run on an older, cheaper GPU with little latency cost while the prompt phase can't?
How does sending KV layer by layer hide most of the transfer, and what is left exposed?
In Dynamo's router, when does a cache-hot worker lose to a cold one?
What does conditional disaggregation do with a short or already-cached prompt, and why?
Which of Kiely's three conditions does the course's Llama-3.1-70B example fail?

must: The prompt phase is compute-bound and the token phase memory-bound → the H100 halves prompt time (0.51–0.54×) but only takes 30–40% off token time while costing more per hour → put the token phase on cheaper (A100) or power-capped GPUs → better cost and energy per request

Send each layer's KV as soon as that layer finishes → the transfer overlaps the remaining layers' compute → only the tail is exposed (~5 ms on H100, 0.8% of end-to-end vs up to 3% serialized) → cross-node transfer becomes cheap enough for production

Router cost = scaled uncached prefill blocks (after cache-hit credit) + active decode blocks → a cache hit shrinks the prefill term, load grows the decode term → the lowest total wins, so a busy cache-hot worker can lose to an idle cold one → neither load-only nor cache-only routing

Disaggregation adds a transfer, a second queue and idle prefill memory → it only pays with large volume (100M–1B tokens/day), big models (≥ 100B) and prefill-heavy traffic → otherwise replicas with chunked prefill and prefix caching win; conditional disaggregation prefills short or cached prompts locally
elevated: The best P:D ratio moves with traffic (1:1 on Mooncake's trace, 2:1 in DistServe's Fig 1, 3:1 in the Scaling Book) → a fixed xPyD lets the prefill queue grow or decode run out of KV → Dynamo's planner resizes each pool, predicting load because a worker takes minutes to start
reference: Splitwise's seven insights, Table IV values and the cluster design names
Dynamo README headline numbers (30×, 7×, 750×) and where each appears
metric aliases: TPOT, TBT, ITL, TPS, goodput variants

compress.prompt: From memory, write four one-line answers: which hardware per phase (Splitwise), where the KV lives (Mooncake), how work is routed and pools resized (Dynamo), and whether to do it at all (Kiely). Then draw the router's cost as one formula.
checklist: prompt phase on the fast GPU, token phase on cheaper or power-capped GPUs
layer-wise transfer hides most of the KV move
shared DRAM/SSD KV pool so reused prefixes load instead of recompute
route by cache hits and load together; resize xPyD with a planner
only for high volume, ≥ 100B models and prefill-heavy traffic; otherwise conditional or none

retrieve.q: Explain why Splitwise concludes that A100s are as good or better than H100s for the token phase, using what bounds each phase.
answer: the token phase is limited by memory, not compute
so the H100's extra compute barely helps it (TBT 40 → 28 ms conversation, 52 → 31 coding) while its hourly price is much higher
Table IV: cost per request $2.4 on A100 vs $3.6 on H100 for conversation, with energy 7.9 vs 9.4 Whr

retrieve.q: Walk through Dynamo's router choosing between worker A (50 active prefill blocks, 300 decode blocks, 30 of the prompt's 40 blocks cached) and worker B (idle prefill, 150 decode blocks, nothing cached), with scale 1.
answer: B wins even though A holds the cache, because A's load dominates

retrieve.q: A team serves a 70B model at 300M tokens a day with short chat prompts and asks whether to adopt Dynamo's disaggregation. What do you tell them, citing the thresholds?
answer: 300M tokens a day is ≈ 3,472 tok/s, inside Kiely's 100M–1B band, so volume is borderline
so: replicas with chunked prefill and prefix caching first; Dynamo's own docs note aggregated workers often win at low concurrency

compare.q: Splitwise vs DistServe: both split phases. Which resource does each optimise, and which design choice follows from that?
answer: DistServe maximises goodput per GPU under SLOs, so it searches parallelism per phase on identical GPUs
Splitwise optimises throughput per dollar and per watt, so it puts phases on different GPU types or power caps
DistServe keeps KV on NVLink by placement; Splitwise overlaps an InfiniBand transfer layer by layer

compare.q: Mooncake's Conductor vs Dynamo's KV-aware router: what do both add into one cost, and what does each add beyond routing?
answer: both trade cache reuse against queue/load instead of using either alone
Mooncake estimates time to first token (transfer + queue + uncached prefill) and rejects requests that can't meet SLOs
Dynamo scores blocks, then adds a planner that resizes pools and a tiered KV block manager

predict.q: Dynamo's launch blog reported more than 2× for Llama 70B on Hopper at input/output 3K/50, although 70B fails Kiely's ≥ 100B condition. Which feature of that workload explains it? Commit first.
predict.answer: The shape: 3,000 input tokens and only 50 output tokens is extremely prefill-heavy (60:1), which is Kiely's third condition in its strongest form. Long prefills would stall a colocated decode batch on every request, so separating them pays even for a sub-100B model. The thresholds are rules of thumb, and workload shape can override model size.

apply.task: Decide for three workloads, using Kiely's three conditions and the card's numbers: (a) Llama-3.1-70B, 300M tokens/day, 1,000 in / 300 out; (b) DeepSeek-V3/R1 at DeepSeek's Day 6 volume (608B in, 168B out per day); (c) a 671B MoE at 50M tokens/day for an internal tool. Convert each volume to tokens per second, mark each condition pass/fail, and give a verdict (disaggregate, conditional, or replicas).
apply.done: You have a 3 × 3 pass/fail table, tokens per second for each, and a verdict with one reason each.
apply.hint: (a) ≈ 3,472 tok/s, borderline volume, fails size, not prefill-heavy (3.3:1 is moderate) → replicas + chunked prefill. (b) 776B/day ≈ 8.98M tok/s, passes all three (671B, 3.6:1) → disaggregate. (c) 50M/day ≈ 579 tok/s, fails volume → replicas, even though the model is huge.
